[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Accelerating PyTorch Models with torch.compile and the Inductor Backend"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"PyTorch 2.x introduced a revolutionary way to speed up deep learning models without modifying your source code significantly. At the core of this release is torch.compile, powered by the default Inductor compiler backend. This tutorial covers how to leverage these features for maximum performance."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding torch.compile"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The torch.compile function uses Python's frame evaluation API to capture graphs, run graph-level optimizations, and lower operations down to high-performance kernels. Instead of eagerly executing operations line-by-line, it fuses operations together to reduce memory overhead and kernel launch latency."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Basic Usage"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"To compile an existing PyTorch module, you simply pass it to torch.compile. The function returns a compiled module that can be used identically to the original module."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torchvision.models as models

# Initialize a standard model
model = models.resnet50(pretrained=False).cuda()

# Compile the model using torch.compile
optimized_model = torch.compile(model)

# Run inference
inputs = torch.randn(16, 3, 224, 224).cuda()
outputs = optimized_model(inputs)
print(outputs.shape)"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Choosing the Right Backend: Inductor"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"PyTorch supports multiple compiler backends, but Inductor is the default and most mature option. Inductor generates optimized Triton kernels for GPUs and C++ kernels for CPUs. You can explicitly specify the backend via the backend parameter, though it defaults to inductor."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"# Explicitly specifying the inductor backend
optimized_model = torch.compile(model, backend="inductor")"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Modes for Compilation"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"torch.compile provides preset modes to balance compilation time against runtime performance:"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"mode="default": Balances fast compilation time with reasonable runtime performance."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"mode="reduce-overhead": Uses CUDA graphs to reduce framework overhead for smaller batch sizes, increasing memory usage."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"mode="max-autotune": Runs extensive benchmarking to find the absolute fastest kernels, resulting in a very long initial compilation time."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"# Using max-autotune mode for maximum performance
optimized_model = torch.compile(model, mode="max-autotune")"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Handling Dynamic Shapes"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, torch.compile specializes shapes based on the first input it receives. If your batch size or sequence length changes frequently, this can cause excessive recompilations. You can set dynamic=True to handle varying shapes gracefully."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"# Enabling dynamic shapes to prevent recompilation on varying batch sizes
optimized_model = torch.compile(model, dynamic=True)"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices and Troubleshooting"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Warm-up iterations: The first few runs include compilation overhead. Always benchmark after a few warm-up steps."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Python side-effects: Avoid mutating global state or performing heavy CPU-bound Python operations inside the compiled region."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Debugging guards: Use TORCH_LOGS="graph_breaks" environment variable to debug why your model falls back to eager execution."}]
